title: Plan Days by Their Hardest Task
statement:
You have a list of tasks that must be done in the given order; effort[i] is how hard task i is. You will spread them over exactly days days, and every day you must finish at least one task. So the plan cuts the list into days non-empty consecutive groups.

A day is as tiring as the hardest task done that day. Return the smallest possible sum of daily tiredness over the whole plan, or -1 if there are fewer tasks than days.

examples.why: Day one does 7, 1, 1, 5 (hardest 7), day two does 2: 7 + 2 = 9. Putting the 7 alone on day one looks natural but costs 7 + 5 = 12.
[2] [9, 3, 8] [1] costs 2 + 9 + 1. Keeping the two hard tasks on the same day means paying for only one of them.
Two tasks cannot fill three days.

hints: Decide the last day first. If the last day does tasks j…n−1, what is left to solve?
Let best(k, i) be the cheapest way to do the first i tasks in k days. The last of those k days does tasks j…i−1 for some j, and costs max(effort[j..i−1]).
best(k, i) = min over j of best(k−1, j) + max(effort[j..i−1]). Loop j downward from i−1 so the running maximum of the last day grows by one task at a time.

explain.intuition:
Greedy ideas fail here: isolating the hardest task can be worse than grouping it with another hard one, as both examples show. What does work is to fix where the last day starts. If it covers tasks j…i−1, it costs their maximum, and the earlier days face the same problem on the shorter list 0…j−1 with one day fewer.

So define dp[k][i] as the least total for doing the first i tasks in k days. Then dp[k][i] = min over j of dp[k−1][j] + max(effort[j..i−1]), where j ≥ k−1 so the earlier days each still get a task. If you walk j from i−1 downward, the maximum of the last day is a running maximum, so each table cell costs O(n).
steps: Set dp[0][0] = 0 and every other entry to infinity.
For k from 1 to days and i from k to n: walk j from i − 1 down to k − 1, keeping top = max(effort[j..i−1]), and take the minimum of dp[k−1][j] + top.
pitfalls: Putting the hardest task alone on its own day. It often pays to group hard tasks together.
Letting earlier days end up empty. The split point j must leave at least one task for each earlier day.
Forgetting the impossible case and returning infinity or 0 when there are fewer tasks than days.

complexity.space: O(days · n), or O(n) keeping two rows

solutions.title: Try every way to cut
solutions.idea: Recursively choose how many tasks the current day takes, then plan the rest with one day fewer.

solutions.title: Table over days and tasks
solutions.idea: dp[k][i] = cheapest plan for the first i tasks in k days; the last day covers j…i−1 and its cost is a running maximum as j moves left.

followups: With n up to 100 000 the O(n²) per day is too slow. How can a monotonic stack bring each day down to O(n)?
Each day may hold at most m tasks. What changes in the recurrence?
